newsitem.title: USA: Proposed SEC fee rollback gets White House support.
newsitem.headline: Proposed SEC fee rollback gets White House support.

text.p: The Clinton administration now supports a proposed $850 million, 10-year fee rollback for the Securities and Exchange Commission, a spokesman for the Office of Mangement and Budget said Tuesday.
"We support the proposal," said Larry Haas, OMB associate director for communications.

The proposal was agreed to Monday night by House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, R-Va., and Sen. Fritz Hollings, the South Carolina Democrat who leads the Senate conferees reconciling House and Senate versions of a bill designed to deregulate the securities industry.
The House version of the bill had originally called for a $700 million fee rollback over five years.
The proposal was part of a scheme to allow the SEC to be less reliant on fees for its funding.
Instead, Congress would include the SEC in the normal budgetary process in a move to eliminate snags in when its funding comes up for Congressional action each year.
The OMB had opposed the rollback initially, noting that under the proposed budget scheme, the SEC would have to compete with other agencies in seeking funding.
Haas did not say why the OMB had change its stand. But he said that the budget office will now "do everything we can to be helpful" in getting the securities bill passed.
"It's our hope that we can get it done" he said. The current congressional term adjourns Sept. 27.
An SEC spokeswoman said the agency had no comment at this time on fee proposal.
The fee rollback is a crucial issue that has stalled consideration of the bill, which seeks to eliminate duplicative securities regulations enforced by the SEC and state regulators.
The bill will also give the SEC more powers to regulate and lessen state regulators' role in the mutual fund industry.
A spokesman for Bliley said other issues remained to be resolved, including regulation of investment advisers, which is a major provision in the Senate version.
"The remaining issues are minor, compared to the fee rollback," the spokesman said.
The House Commerce Committee estimated that the rollback would generate savings of $850 million for the first 10 years and $835 million in the the 11th year.

Under the proposal, SEC's registration fees would be reduced from the current 1/29th of 1 percent to 1/33 of 1 percent from the first year, to 1/50th of 1 percent in 2006 and to 1/150th of 1 percent in the year 2007, the panel said.
At the same time, stock transaction fees would now include Nasdaq trades, at 1/300th of 1 percent, until 2006 and then reduced to 1/800th of 1 percent by 2007, it said.
